[[de:Kokutai]][[en:Kokutai]][[es:Kokutai]][[fa:کوکوتای]][[fi:Kokutai]][[fr:Kokutai]][[id:Kokutai]][[it:Kokutai]][[ja:国体]][[ko:국체론]][[nl:Kokutai]][[ru:Кокутай]][[tr:Kokutai]][[uk:Кокутай]][[zh-min-nan:Kok-thé]] [[de:Kokutai]][[en:Kokutai]][[es:Kokutai]][[fa:کوکوتای]][[fi:Kokutai]][[fr:Kokutai]][[id:Kokutai]][[it:Kokutai]][[ja:国体]][[ko:국체론]][[nl:Kokutai]][[ru:Кокутай]][[tr:Kokutai]][[uk:Кокутай]][[zh-min-nan:Kok-thé]] [[de:Kokutai]][[en:Kokutai]][[es:Kokutai]][[fa:کوکوتای]][[fi:Kokutai]][[fr:Kokutai]][[id:Kokutai]][[it:Kokutai]][[ja:国体]][[ko:국체론]][[nl:Kokutai]][[ru:Кокутай]][[tr:Kokutai]][[uk:Кокутай]][[zh-min-nan:Kok-thé]] {{Short description|Japanese political concept}} {{Other uses}} {{Italic title|reason=}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2020}} [[File:Founding_of_the_Nation_by_Kawamura_Kiyoo.jpg|thumb|The nationalistic essence of ''kokutai'' is thought of as the uniqueness of the Japanese {{ill|Polity|en|Polity|WD=Q1063239|lt=Polity}} as issuing from a leader of {{ill|Family tree of Japanese monarchs|en|Family tree of Japanese monarchs|WD=Q3249915|lt=divine origin}}.{{ref|a}}]] {{nihongo|'''''Kokutai'''''|国体||"national body/structure of state"}} is a concept in the {{ill|Japanese language|en|Japanese language|WD=Q5287|lt=Japanese language}} translatable as "[[:en:system of government|system of government]]", "{{ill|Sovereignty|en|Sovereignty|WD=Q42008|lt=Sovereignty}}", "national identity, essence and character", "national polity; {{ill|body politic|en|body politic|WD=Q4936955|lt=body politic}}; national entity; basis for the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor's}} sovereignty; [[:en:Japanese constitution|Japanese constitution]]" or {{ill|Nation|en|Nation|WD=Q6266|lt=Nation}}. ==Etymology== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2023}} ''Kokutai'' originated as a {{ill|Sino-Japanese vocabulary|en|Sino-Japanese vocabulary|WD=Q4222379|lt=Sino-Japanese loanword}} from Chinese ''guoti'' ({{zh|c={{linktext|國體}}|p=guótǐ}}; "state political system; national governmental structure"). The Japanese {{ill|Compound (linguistics)|en|Compound (linguistics)|WD=Q245423|lt=compound word}} joins {{nihongo4||國|koku|"country; nation; province; land"}} and {{nihongo4||體|tai|"body; substance; object; structure; form; style"}}. According to the ''{{ill|Hanyu Da Cidian|en|Hanyu Da Cidian|WD=Q1138917|lt=Hanyu Da Cidian}}'', the oldest ''guoti'' usages are in two [[:en:Chinese classic texts|Chinese classic texts]]. The 2nd century BC ''Guliang zhuan'' ({{zh|c=榖梁傳|l=Guliang's Commentary|labels=no}}) to the {{ill|Spring and Autumn Annals|en|Spring and Autumn Annals|WD=Q747720|lt=Spring and Autumn Annals}} glosses ''dafu'' ({{zh|c=大夫|l=high minister; senior official|labels=no}}) as ''guoti'' metaphorically meaning "embodiment of the country". The 1st century AD ''{{ill|Book of Han|en|Book of Han|WD=Q846905|lt=Book of Han}}'' history of {{ill|Emperor Cheng of Han|en|Emperor Cheng of Han|WD=Q7234|lt=Emperor Cheng of Han}} used ''guoti'' to mean "laws and governance" of Confucianist officials. ==Pre-1868== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2023}} The historical origins of ''kokutai'' go back to pre-1868 periods, especially the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} ruled by the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] (1603–1868). {{ill|Aizawa Seishisai|en|Aizawa Seishisai|WD=Q2090901|lt=Aizawa Seishisai}} (会沢正志斎, 1782–1863) was an authority on {{ill|Neo-Confucianism|en|Neo-Confucianism|WD=Q825754|lt=Neo-Confucianism}} and leader of the {{ill|Mitogaku|en|Mitogaku|WD=Q260529|lt=Mitogaku}} (水戸学 "Mito School") that supported direct restoration of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=Imperial House of Japan}}. He popularized the word ''kokutai'' in his 1825 ''Shinron'' (新論 "New Theses"), which also introduced the term ''[[Sonnō jōi]]'' ("revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians"). Aizawa developed his ideas of ''kokutai'' using the idea that the Japanese national myths in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' were historical facts, believing that the Emperor was directly descended from the sun goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]]. Aizawa idealized this divinely-ruled ancient Japan as a form of ''saisei itchi'' (祭政一致 "unity of religion and government") or theocracy. For early Japanese Neo-Confucian scholars, linguist {{ill|Roy Andrew Miller|en|Roy Andrew Miller|WD=Q2676921|lt=Roy Andrew Miller}} (1982:93) says, "''kokutai'' meant something still rather vague and ill defined. It was more or less the Japanese "nation's body" or "national structure". ==From 1868 to 1945== ===From 1868 to 1890=== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2023}} {{ill|Katō Hiroyuki|en|Katō Hiroyuki|WD=Q1960314|lt=Katō Hiroyuki}} (1836–1916) and {{ill|Fukuzawa Yukichi|en|Fukuzawa Yukichi|WD=Q355447|lt=Fukuzawa Yukichi}} (1835–1901) were {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} scholars who analyzed the dominance of Western civilization and urged progress for the Japanese nation. In 1874, Katō wrote the ''Kokutai Shinron'' (国体新論 "New Theory of the National Body/Structure"), which criticized traditional Chinese and Japanese theories of government and, adopting Western theories of {{ill|natural rights|en|natural rights|WD=Q20859012|lt=natural rights}}, proposed a {{ill|Constitutional monarchy|en|Constitutional monarchy|WD=Q41614|lt=Constitutional monarchy}} for Japan. He contrasted between ''kokutai'' and ''seitai'' (政体 "government body/structure"). Brownlee explains.
The ''Kokutai-seitai'' distinction enabled conservatives to identify clearly as ''Kokutai'', National Essence, the "native Japanese", eternal, and immutable aspects of their polity, derived from history, tradition, and custom, and focused on the Emperor. The form of government, ''Seitai'', a secondary concept, then consisted of the historical arrangements for the exercise of political authority. ''Seitai'', the form of government, was historically contingent and changed through time. Japan had experienced in succession direct rule by the Emperors in ancient times, then the rule of the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]] Regents, then seven hundred years of rule by ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}s'', followed by the allegedly direct rule of the Emperors again after the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Each was a ''seitai'', a form of government. In this understanding, the modern system of government under the Meiji Constitution, derived this time from foreign sources, was nothing more than another form of Japanese government, a new ''seitai''. The Constitution was nothing fundamental. (2000:5)
{{ill|Fukuzawa Yukichi|en|Fukuzawa Yukichi|WD=Q355447|lt=Fukuzawa Yukichi}} was an influential author translator for the [[:en:Japanese Embassy to the United States (1860)|Japanese Embassy to the United States (1860)]]. His 1875 "Bunmeiron no Gairyaku" (文明論の概略 "An Outline of a Theory of Civilization") contradicted traditional ideas about ''kokutai''. He reasoned that it was not unique to Japan and that every nation could be said to have a ''kokutai'' "national sovereignty". While Fukuzawa respected the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan}}, he believed ''kokutai'' did not depend upon myths of unbroken descent from Amaterasu. ===Meiji Constitution=== The {{ill|Meiji Constitution|en|Meiji Constitution|WD=Q122804|lt=Constitution of the Empire of Japan}} of 1889 created a form of constitutional monarchy with the ''kokutai'' sovereign emperor and ''seitai'' organs of government. Article 4 declares that "the Emperor is the head of the Empire, combining in Himself the rights of sovereignty", uniting the executive, legislative, and judicial branches of government, although subject to the "consent of the Imperial Diet". This system utilized a democratic form, but in practice was closer to an absolute monarchy. The legal scholar Josefa López notes that under the Meiji Constitution, ''kokutai'' acquired an additional meaning.
The Government created a whole perfect new cultural system around the Tennou [Emperor], and the ''kokutai'' was the expression of it. Moreover, the ''kokutai'' was the basis of the sovereignty. According to Tatsukichi Minobe, ''kokutai'' is understood as the "shape of the Estate" in the sense of "Tenno as the organ of the Estate", while the authoritarians gave the ''kokutai'' a mystical power. The Tennou was a "god" among "humans", the incarnation of the national morals. This notion of ''kokutai'' was extra-juridical, something more cultural than positive. (2006:n.p.)
{{Conservatism in Japan|variants and movements}} This stemmed from drafter [[Itō Hirobumi]]'s rejection of some European notions as unfit for Japan, as they stemmed from European constitutional practice and Christianity.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', pp. 79–80 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} The references to the ''kokutai'' were the justification of the emperor's authority through his divine descent and the unbroken line of emperors, and the unique relationship between subject and sovereign. The "family-state" element in it was given a great deal of prominence by political philosophy.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', p. 80 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} Many conservatives supported these principles as central to '''''Nihon shugi''''' (''Nihon gunkoku shugi'', {{ill|Japanese militarism|en|Japanese militarism|WD=Q702868|lt=Japanese militarism}}), "Japanism", as an alternative to rapid Westernization.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/427 427–428]|quote=Japanists further circumscribed the permissible limits of political discourse. From the middleof the Meiji period, some conservatives had begun to advocate Nihon shugi, or Japanism, as an alternative to rapid Westernization. In particular, they wished to preserve traditional values and what they saw as Japan's unique national polity, or kokutai. For many conservatives in the Meiji era, the concept of the kokutai revolved around two principles. A divine line of emperors had ruled from time immemorial, and intimate familylike ties united the benevolent sovereign with his loyal subjects.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/427}} ''Nihon shugi'' (日本主義, lit. "Japan-ism") is an ideology that values the traditional Japanese spirit and sets the tone of the state and society; it emerged in this period as a reaction to the {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan}}'s radical [[:en:Europeanization|Europeanization]] policy.{{cite web |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E4%B8%BB%E7%BE%A9-110186#E5.A4.A7.E8.BE.9E.E6.9E.97.20.E7.AC.AC.E4.B8.89.E7.89.88 |title=日本主義 |access-date=12 March 2024 |website=kotobank.jp |language=ja }} Nihon shugi is a kind of "''kukka shugi''" (国家主義, lit. "statism" or "nationalism") ideology. ''Nihon Shugi'' opposed 'Europeanism' (欧化主義), '{{ill|Democracy|en|Democracy|WD=Q7174|lt=Democracy}}' and '{{ill|Socialism|en|Socialism|WD=Q7272|lt=Socialism}}', which were considered unrelated to Japanese traditions, and during the {{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taishō}} and {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era}}, it emphasized the ''Kokutai'' ideology centered on the emperor as opposed to {{ill|Marxism|en|Marxism|WD=Q7264|lt=Marxism}}. ===Taishō Democracy=== From the [[:en:Xinhai Revolution|Xinhai Revolution]] to the enactment of the {{ill|Peace Preservation Law|en|Peace Preservation Law|WD=Q657216|lt=Peace Preservation Law}} (1911–1925), the most important pre-World War II democracy movement "[[:en:Taisho Democracy|Taishō Democracy]]" occurred. During the Taishō Democracy, the political theorist {{ill|Sakuzō Yoshino|en|Sakuzō Yoshino|WD=Q1186931|lt=Sakuzō Yoshino}} (1878–1933) rejected Western democracy ''minshu shugi'' (民主主義 lit. "people rule principle/-ism") and proposed a compromise on imperial democracy ''minpon shugi'' (民本主義 "people based principle/-ism"). However, as {{ill|Japanese nationalism|en|Japanese nationalism|WD=Q1331440|lt=Japanese nationalism}} grew, questions arose whether the ''kokutai'' emperor could be limited by the ''seitai'' government. The {{ill|Peace Preservation Law|en|Peace Preservation Law|WD=Q657216|lt=Peace Preservation Law}} of 1925 forbade both forming and belonging to any organization that proposed altering the ''kokutai'' or the abolishment of private property, effectively criminalizing socialism, communism, {{ill|Republicanism|en|Republicanism|WD=Q877848|lt=Republicanism}}, democracy and other anti-Tenno [[:en:ideologies|ideologies]].{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/390 390]|quote=At the same time that [the government] approved universal manhood suffrage, the Diet passed the Peace Preservation Law of 1925. Drafted by bureaucrats within the Ministry of Justice, the measure stipulated that anyone "who organizes a group for the purpose of changing the national polity (kokutai) or of denying the private property system, or anyone who knowingly participates in such group" could be jailed for ten years, or even executed after the law was amended three years later.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/390}} The [[:en:Tokubetsu Kōtō Keisatsu|Tokkō]] ("Special Higher Police") was established as a type of {{ill|Thought Police|en|Thought Police|WD=Q1264653|lt=Thought Police}} to investigate political groups that might threaten Tenno-centered social order of Japan.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', p. 184 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} ===World War II usage=== {{ill|Tatsukichi Minobe|en|Tatsukichi Minobe|WD=Q709643|lt=Tatsukichi Minobe}} (1873–1948), a professor emeritus of law at {{ill|University of Tokyo|en|University of Tokyo|WD=Q7842|lt=Tokyo Imperial University}}, theorized that under the Meiji Constitution, the emperor was an organ of the state and not a sacrosanct power beyond the state.{{ill|Andrew Gordon (historian)|en|Andrew Gordon (historian)|WD=Q4757131|lt=Andrew Gordon}}, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', pp. 198–199, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} This was regarded as ''{{ill|Lèse-majesté|en|Lèse-majesté|WD=Q1134057|lt=Lèse-majesté}}''.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/428 428]|quote=In the 1930s, however, Japanists singled out Minobe for intense criticism. Battle was joined in 1934 when rightwing organizations, including the Imperial Military Reservists' Association, published accusatory books and pamphlets charging that Minobe's thoughts amounted to Ièse majesté.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/428}} Minobe was appointed to the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers}} in 1932 but forced to resign after an assassination attempt and vehement criticisms that he was disloyal to the emperor.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', p. 199, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} Great efforts were made to foment a "Japanese spirit" even in popular culture, as in the promotion of the "{{ill|Ode of Showa Restoration|en|Ode of Showa Restoration|WD=Q30947150|lt=Song of Young Japan}}."{{ill|Piers Brendon|en|Piers Brendon|WD=Q15458673|lt=Piers Brendon}}, ''The Dark Valley: A Panorama of the 1930s'', p. 441 {{ISBN|0-375-40881-9}}
Brave warriors united in justice In spirit a match for a million – Ready like the myriad {{ill|Cherry blossom|en|Cherry blossom|WD=Q871991|lt=Cherry blossom}}s to scatter In the spring sky of the {{ill|Shōwa Restoration|en|Shōwa Restoration|WD=Q863412|lt=Shōwa Restoration}}.
The national debates over ''kokutai'' led the Prime Minister Prince {{ill|Fumimaro Konoe|en|Fumimaro Konoe|WD=Q315594|lt=Fumimaro Konoe}} to appoint a committee of Japan's leading professors to deliberate the matter. In 1937, they issued the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' (国体の本義, "Cardinal Principles of the National Body/Structure", see Gauntlett and Hall 1949). Miller gives this description.
The document known as the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' was actually a pamphlet of 156 pages, an official publication of the {{ill|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|en|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|WD=Q1054379|lt=Japanese Ministry of Education}}, first issued in March 1937 and eventually circulated in millions of copies throughout the home islands and the empire. It contained the official teaching of the Japanese state on every aspect of domestic policy, international affairs, culture, and civilization. (1982:92)
It clearly stated its purpose: to overcome social unrest and to develop a new Japan.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/465 465–466]|quote=Besides hushing its critics, the government sought to inculcate good citizenship among schoolchildren by introducing a new textbook, Kokutai no hongi ("Cardinal Principles of the National Polity"), published by the Ministry of Education on March 30, 1937, as an official statement of the government's concept of the kokutai. The purpose of the text, according to its own conclusion, was to overcome social unrest and "develop a new Japan by virtue of the Way of the Empire which stands firm throughout the ages at home and abroad, and thereby more than ever to guard and maintain the prosperity of the Imperial Throne which is coeval with heaven and earth." Following a historical overview that paid special honor to the divine origins of the imperial line, a series of overtly nationalistic essays explored the vlrtues of Japan's "special and unique" customs, culture, religion, morality, and way of life. Throughout the volume, the prose sang the praises of the national achievements of the past, credited those accomplishments to the wisdom of the imperial house, and called upon the Japanese of the 1930s to prepare themselves to make any sacrifice necessary to preserve the integrity of the emperor and nation.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/465}} From this pamphlet, pupils were taught to put the nation before the self, and that they were part of the state and not separate from it.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', p. 187 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} It also instructed them in the principle of [[hakkō ichiu]] ("eight cords, one roof"), which would be used to justify imperialism.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/470 470]|quote=Konoe and Matsuoka added to the allure of a geographically extended coprosperity sphere by wrapping it in imperial shrouds. Any move south, they averred, would be accomplished "peacefully" and in accordance, as Konoe so carefully phrased it in his radio address, "with the lofty spirit of hakko ichiu." It was another skillful rhetorical flourish by the veteran wordsmith. As every Japanese schoolchild who had read Kokutai no hongi knew by heart, hakko ichiu meant "eight cords, one roof" and first appeared in the eighth-century chronicle [[Nihon Shoki]] to describe how the legendary first emperor Jimmu extended his dominion over the other clans of the early Japanese islands, which subsequently enjoyed unparalleled prosperity and security thanks to his imperial benevolence. Superimposed upon Asia in 1940, the resuscitated ideal pictured a quasi family of nations led by Japan and its patriarch-emperor; the "Imperial Way," Matsuoka intoned, would permit "every nation and every race" to find "its proper place in the world."|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/470}} Brownlee concludes that after the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' proclamation,
It is clear that at this stage in history, they were no longer dealing with a concept to generate spiritual unity like Aizawa Seishisai in 1825, or with a political theory of Japan designed to accommodate modern institutions of government, like the Meiji Constitution. The committee of professors from prestigious universities sought to define the essential truths of Japan, which might be termed religious, or even metaphysical, because they required faith at the expense of logic and reason. (2006:13)
The Ministry of Education promulgated it throughout the school system. By 1937, "election purification", originally aimed at corruption, required that no candidate set the people in opposition to either the military or the bureaucracy.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', p. 196, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} This was required because voters were required to support imperial rule. Some objections to the founding of the ''Taisei Yokusankai'' or {{ill|Imperial Rule Assistance Association|en|Imperial Rule Assistance Association|WD=Q714797|lt=Imperial Rule Assistance Association}}, came on the grounds that ''kokutai'' already required all imperial subjects to support imperial rule. Conservative thinkers voiced concerns that the establishment of an empowered class of aides to the emperor was akin to the creation of a new shogunate.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/454 454]|quote=Conservatives such as Hiranuma Kiichiro, who served as prime minister for eight months in 1939, objected that the proposed totalitarian IRAA was nothing but a "new shogunate" that would usurp the power of the emperor's government, and Japanists declared that the national polity, the hallowed kokutai, already united the emperor with subjects who naturally fulfilled their sacred obligation to "assist imperial rule." On a more mundane plane, senior officials within the Home Ministry feared the loss of bureaucratic turf and complained that the proposed network of occupationally based units would interfere with local administration at a particularly crucial time in the nation's history.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/454}} For the leaders of Japan's "fascist-nationalist clique", writes Miller (1982:93), "''kokutai'' had become a convenient term for indicating all the ways in which they believed that the Japanese nation, as a political as well as a racial entity, was simultaneously different from and superior to all other nations on earth." This term, and what it meant, were widely inculcated in propaganda.Anthony Rhodes, ''Propaganda: The art of persuasion: World War II'', p. 246, 1976, Chelsea House Publishers, New York The final letters of {{ill|Kamikaze|en|Kamikaze|WD=Q133194|lt=Kamikaze}} pilots expressed, above all, that their motivations were gratitude to Japan and to its Emperor as the embodiment of ''kokutai''.{{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris}}, ''The Nobility of Failure: Tragic Heroes in the History of Japan'', p. 309 Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1975 {{ISBN?}} A sailor might give his life to save the picture of the Emperor on a submarine.{{ill|Masanori Ito (journalist)|en|Masanori Ito (journalist)|WD=Q10885109|lt=Masanori Ito}}, ''The End of the Imperial Japanese Navy'' p. 28, New York W.W. Norton & Company, 1956 During World War II, some anti-{{ill|Modernism|en|Modernism|WD=Q878985|lt=modernist}} intellectuals argued that prior to the [[Meiji Restoration]], Japan was always a classless society under a benevolent emperor, but the restoration had plunged the nation into Western materialism (an argument that ignored commercialism and ribald culture in the Tokugawa era), which had caused people to forget their nature. To recover their traditional identity, Japanese citizens had to actively participate in the war effort.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', pp. 219–220, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} "Japanist" unions endeavoured to win support by disavowing class violence and pledging support for nation and emperor.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/467 467]|quote=The growing sense of national emergency prompted many groups that earlier had assumed an oppositional stance toward the state to reassess their goals and tactics. One expression of that tendency came in the early 1930s, when thousands of workers joined so-called Japanist unions whose leadership hoped to improve working conditions by disavowing violent confrontations and demonstrating their loyalty to nation and emperor. Kamino Shin'ichi, originally a foreman at the lshikawajima shipyards, organized one of the more influential Japanist unions. In concert with other members of the conservative right, he and his followers ridiculed the political parties as being corrupt, condemned liberalism and democracy as the failed ideologies of a decadent West, and sought to build a new industrial order, premised on the "unity of emperor and subject," in which laborers and capitalists would be "of one mind and spirit, fused in an inseparable solidarity."|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/467}} Nevertheless, because of the mistrust of unions in such unity, the Japanese went to replace them with "councils" in every factory, containing both management and worker representatives to contain conflict.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', pp. 195–196, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} Like the Nazi councils they were copying, this was part of a program to create a classless national unity. Because many religions had figures that distracted from the central emperor, they were attacked, such as the [[Oomoto]] sect condemned for worshipping figures other than [[Amaterasu]], and in 1939, the Religious Organization authorized the shutting down of any religion that did not conform to the Imperial Way, which the authorities promptly used.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/469 469]|quote=No group experienced more severe suppression than the new religions as Home Ministry bureaucrats embarked upon a crusade "to eradicate evil cults" for the crime of propagating Iese majeste. As manifested in such works as kokutai no hongi, the government in the 1930s fostered the growth of an official orthodoxy centered upon a sacrosanct emperor who stood both as the head of state and as the benevolent father of the family of Japanese citizens. Although not overtly antiemperor, many of the new religions espoused doctrines that threatened the centrality of the imperial figure; prosecutors, for instance, condemned the Omoto sect for revering deities other than the Sun Goddess. The most dramatic moment in the government's campaign against "quack religions" came on December 8, 1935, when hundreds of police stormed Omoto headquarters, smashed the main shrine building, dynamited an auxiliary hall, decapitated religious statues, and arrested nearly a thousand sect members. Four years later the Diet passed the Religious Organizations Law empowering the government to disband any religious organization whose teachings did not conform with "The Imperial Way," and officials promptly suppressed other unorthodox religions. An aversion for social disorder and a desire to "unify the will of the people" around national goals prompted bureaucratic officials in the 1930s to suppress or to co-opt the support of organizations that opposed government policies. Some of the associations, notably the Omoto sect, preferred to break rather than to bend, but most tempered their demands, shifted to less contentious goals, or even dissolved themselves.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/469}} Hirohito evoked the ''Kokutai'' in his {{ill|Hirohito surrender broadcast|en|Hirohito surrender broadcast|WD=Q709465|lt=surrender broadcast}}, which announced the Japanese acceptance of the {{ill|Potsdam Declaration|en|Potsdam Declaration|WD=Q163244|lt=Potsdam Declaration}} (unconditional surrender). ==Post-1945== By the {{ill|Surrender of Japan|en|Surrender of Japan|WD=Q6540361|lt=Surrender of Japan}} in 1945, the significance of ''kokutai'' diminished. In autumn 1945, [[:en:Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers|GHQ]] forbade circulation of the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' and on 15 October repealed the 1925 {{ill|Peace Preservation Law|en|Peace Preservation Law|WD=Q657216|lt=Peace Preservation Law}}. By the enactment of the {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|WD=Q237082|lt=Constitution of the State of Japan}} (3 May 1947), {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Tenno}}'s sovereignty and the ''lèse-majesté'' were repealed. Nevertheless, some authors, including Miller (1982:95), believe that traces of Japanese ''kokutai'' "are quite as vivid today as they ever were". In the 21st century, Japanese nationalists, such as those affiliated with the {{ill|Nippon Kaigi|en|Nippon Kaigi|WD=Q11507216|lt=Nippon Kaigi}} lobby, have begun using the phrase "kunigara" (国柄, "national character"). == Notes == :1.{{note|a}}In the illustration is the "Tokoyo no Naganakidori" (常世之長鳴鳥), a long-singing [[:en:cockerel|cockerel]] from the {{illm|Everlasting Land|ja|常世の国}} which appears in the [[Kojiki]] as the herald of Amaterasu. == See also == {{Portal|Japan}} *''{{ill|An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus|en|An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus|WD=Q4750110|lt=An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus}}'' *{{ill|Gekokujō|en|Gekokujō|WD=Q2416571|lt=Gekokujō}} *[[Imperial Rescript on Education]] *{{ill|Japanese Historical Text Initiative|en|Japanese Historical Text Initiative|WD=Q16973361|lt=Japanese Historical Text Initiative}} *{{ill|Hirohito surrender broadcast|en|Hirohito surrender broadcast|WD=Q709465|lt=Hirohito surrender broadcast}} (Gyokuon-hōsō) *{{ill|Kokuchūkai|en|Kokuchūkai|WD=Q11420994|lt=Kokuchūkai}} (Column of the Nation Society) *[[National Spiritual Mobilization Movement]] *[[Shinbutsu-shūgō]] *[[:en:Socialist thought in Imperial Japan|Socialist thought in Imperial Japan]] *[[:en:Statism in Shōwa Japan|Statism in Shōwa Japan]] *{{ill|Uyoku dantai|en|Uyoku dantai|WD=Q181924|lt=Uyoku dantai}} (Nationalist groups of Japan) *{{ill|Yangmingism|en|Yangmingism|WD=Q697205|lt=Yangmingism}} *{{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}} == References == {{reflist}} * Brownlee, John S. "[http://www.adilegian.com/PDF/brownlee.pdf Four Stages of the Japanese Kokutai (National Essence)]", 2000. * Daikichi, Irokawa. ''The Culture of the Meiji Period''. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1970. * Gauntlett, John Owen and Hall, Robert King. ''Kokutai no hongi: cardinal principles of the national entity of Japan''. Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University press, 1949. * {{ill|Joseph Kitagawa|en|Joseph Kitagawa|WD=Q3185165|lt=Kitagawa, Joseph M.}} "The Japanese ''Kokutai'' (National Community) History and Myth", ''History of Religions'', Vol. 13.3 (Feb., 1974), pp. 209–226. * Valderrama López, Josefa. "[http://seneca.uab.cat/hmic/2006/orientats/Kokutai.pdf Beyond words: the "kokutai" and its background]{{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}". ''Història Moderna i Contemporània'', 2006. {{ISSN|1696-4403}}. * Miller, Roy Andrew. ''Japan's Modern Myth''. New York: Weatherhill, 1982. * Antoni, Klaus ''Kokutai – Political Shintô from Early-Modern to Contemporary Japan''. Eberhard Karls University Tuebingen, Tobias-lib 2016. {{ISBN|978-3-946552-00-0}}. [[de:Kokutai]][[en:Kokutai]][[es:Kokutai]][[fa:کوکوتای]][[fi:Kokutai]][[fr:Kokutai]][[id:Kokutai]][[it:Kokutai]][[ja:国体]][[ko:국체론]][[nl:Kokutai]][[ru:Кокутай]][[tr:Kokutai]][[uk:Кокутай]][[zh-min-nan:Kok-thé]] [[de:Kokutai]][[en:Kokutai]][[es:Kokutai]][[fa:کوکوتای]][[fi:Kokutai]][[fr:Kokutai]][[id:Kokutai]][[it:Kokutai]][[ja:国体]][[ko:국체론]][[nl:Kokutai]][[ru:Кокутай]][[tr:Kokutai]][[uk:Кокутай]][[zh-min-nan:Kok-thé]] [[de:Kokutai]][[en:Kokutai]][[es:Kokutai]][[fa:کوکوتای]][[fi:Kokutai]][[fr:Kokutai]][[id:Kokutai]][[it:Kokutai]][[ja:国体]][[ko:국체론]][[nl:Kokutai]][[ru:Кокутай]][[tr:Kokutai]][[uk:Кокутай]][[zh-min-nan:Kok-thé]] {{Short description|Japanese political concept}} {{Other uses}} {{Italic title|reason=}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2020}} [[File:Founding_of_the_Nation_by_Kawamura_Kiyoo.jpg|thumb|The nationalistic essence of ''kokutai'' is thought of as the uniqueness of the Japanese {{ill|Polity|en|Polity|WD=Q1063239|lt=Polity|1=Polity}} as issuing from a leader of {{ill|Family tree of Japanese monarchs|en|Family tree of Japanese monarchs|WD=Q3249915|lt=divine origin|1=Family tree of Japanese monarchs}}.{{ref|a}}]] {{nihongo|'''''Kokutai'''''|国体||"national body/structure of state"}} is a concept in the {{ill|Japanese language|en|Japanese language|WD=Q5287|lt=Japanese language|1=Japanese language}} translatable as "[[:en:system of government|system of government]]", "{{ill|Sovereignty|en|Sovereignty|WD=Q42008|lt=Sovereignty|1=Sovereignty}}", "national identity, essence and character", "national polity; {{ill|body politic|en|body politic|WD=Q4936955|lt=body politic|1=Body politic}}; national entity; basis for the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor's|1=Emperor of Japan}} sovereignty; [[:en:Japanese constitution|Japanese constitution]]" or {{ill|Nation|en|Nation|WD=Q6266|lt=Nation|1=Nation}}. ==Etymology== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2023}} ''Kokutai'' originated as a {{ill|Sino-Japanese vocabulary|en|Sino-Japanese vocabulary|WD=Q4222379|lt=Sino-Japanese loanword|1=Sino-Japanese vocabulary}} from Chinese ''guoti'' ({{zh|c={{linktext|國體}}|p=guótǐ}}; "state political system; national governmental structure"). The Japanese {{ill|Compound (linguistics)|en|Compound (linguistics)|WD=Q245423|lt=compound word|1=Compound (linguistics)}} joins {{nihongo4||國|koku|"country; nation; province; land"}} and {{nihongo4||體|tai|"body; substance; object; structure; form; style"}}. According to the ''{{ill|Hanyu Da Cidian|en|Hanyu Da Cidian|WD=Q1138917|lt=Hanyu Da Cidian|1=Hanyu Da Cidian}}'', the oldest ''guoti'' usages are in two [[:en:Chinese classic texts|Chinese classic texts]]. The 2nd century BC ''Guliang zhuan'' ({{zh|c=榖梁傳|l=Guliang's Commentary|labels=no}}) to the {{ill|Spring and Autumn Annals|en|Spring and Autumn Annals|WD=Q747720|lt=Spring and Autumn Annals|1=Spring and Autumn Annals}} glosses ''dafu'' ({{zh|c=大夫|l=high minister; senior official|labels=no}}) as ''guoti'' metaphorically meaning "embodiment of the country". The 1st century AD ''{{ill|Book of Han|en|Book of Han|WD=Q846905|lt=Book of Han|1=Book of Han}}'' history of {{ill|Emperor Cheng of Han|en|Emperor Cheng of Han|WD=Q7234|lt=Emperor Cheng of Han|1=Emperor Cheng of Han}} used ''guoti'' to mean "laws and governance" of Confucianist officials. ==Pre-1868== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2023}} The historical origins of ''kokutai'' go back to pre-1868 periods, especially the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} ruled by the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] (1603–1868). {{ill|Aizawa Seishisai|en|Aizawa Seishisai|WD=Q2090901|lt=Aizawa Seishisai|1=Aizawa Seishisai}} (会沢正志斎, 1782–1863) was an authority on {{ill|Neo-Confucianism|en|Neo-Confucianism|WD=Q825754|lt=Neo-Confucianism|1=Neo-Confucianism}} and leader of the {{ill|Mitogaku|en|Mitogaku|WD=Q260529|lt=Mitogaku|1=Mitogaku}} (水戸学 "Mito School") that supported direct restoration of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=Imperial House of Japan|1=Imperial House of Japan}}. He popularized the word ''kokutai'' in his 1825 ''Shinron'' (新論 "New Theses"), which also introduced the term ''[[Sonnō jōi]]'' ("revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians"). Aizawa developed his ideas of ''kokutai'' using the idea that the Japanese national myths in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' were historical facts, believing that the Emperor was directly descended from the sun goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]]. Aizawa idealized this divinely-ruled ancient Japan as a form of ''saisei itchi'' (祭政一致 "unity of religion and government") or theocracy. For early Japanese Neo-Confucian scholars, linguist {{ill|Roy Andrew Miller|en|Roy Andrew Miller|WD=Q2676921|lt=Roy Andrew Miller|1=Roy Andrew Miller}} (1982:93) says, "''kokutai'' meant something still rather vague and ill defined. It was more or less the Japanese "nation's body" or "national structure". ==From 1868 to 1945== ===From 1868 to 1890=== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2023}} {{ill|Katō Hiroyuki|en|Katō Hiroyuki|WD=Q1960314|lt=Katō Hiroyuki|1=Katō Hiroyuki}} (1836–1916) and {{ill|Fukuzawa Yukichi|en|Fukuzawa Yukichi|WD=Q355447|lt=Fukuzawa Yukichi|1=Fukuzawa Yukichi}} (1835–1901) were {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} scholars who analyzed the dominance of Western civilization and urged progress for the Japanese nation. In 1874, Katō wrote the ''Kokutai Shinron'' (国体新論 "New Theory of the National Body/Structure"), which criticized traditional Chinese and Japanese theories of government and, adopting Western theories of {{ill|natural rights|en|natural rights|WD=Q20859012|lt=natural rights|1=Natural rights}}, proposed a {{ill|Constitutional monarchy|en|Constitutional monarchy|WD=Q41614|lt=Constitutional monarchy|1=Constitutional monarchy}} for Japan. He contrasted between ''kokutai'' and ''seitai'' (政体 "government body/structure"). Brownlee explains.
The ''Kokutai-seitai'' distinction enabled conservatives to identify clearly as ''Kokutai'', National Essence, the "native Japanese", eternal, and immutable aspects of their polity, derived from history, tradition, and custom, and focused on the Emperor. The form of government, ''Seitai'', a secondary concept, then consisted of the historical arrangements for the exercise of political authority. ''Seitai'', the form of government, was historically contingent and changed through time. Japan had experienced in succession direct rule by the Emperors in ancient times, then the rule of the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]] Regents, then seven hundred years of rule by ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}s'', followed by the allegedly direct rule of the Emperors again after the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Each was a ''seitai'', a form of government. In this understanding, the modern system of government under the Meiji Constitution, derived this time from foreign sources, was nothing more than another form of Japanese government, a new ''seitai''. The Constitution was nothing fundamental. (2000:5)
{{ill|Fukuzawa Yukichi|en|Fukuzawa Yukichi|WD=Q355447|lt=Fukuzawa Yukichi|1=Fukuzawa Yukichi}} was an influential author translator for the [[:en:Japanese Embassy to the United States (1860)|Japanese Embassy to the United States (1860)]]. His 1875 "Bunmeiron no Gairyaku" (文明論の概略 "An Outline of a Theory of Civilization") contradicted traditional ideas about ''kokutai''. He reasoned that it was not unique to Japan and that every nation could be said to have a ''kokutai'' "national sovereignty". While Fukuzawa respected the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}}, he believed ''kokutai'' did not depend upon myths of unbroken descent from Amaterasu. ===Meiji Constitution=== The {{ill|Meiji Constitution|en|Meiji Constitution|WD=Q122804|lt=Constitution of the Empire of Japan|1=Meiji Constitution}} of 1889 created a form of constitutional monarchy with the ''kokutai'' sovereign emperor and ''seitai'' organs of government. Article 4 declares that "the Emperor is the head of the Empire, combining in Himself the rights of sovereignty", uniting the executive, legislative, and judicial branches of government, although subject to the "consent of the Imperial Diet". This system utilized a democratic form, but in practice was closer to an absolute monarchy. The legal scholar Josefa López notes that under the Meiji Constitution, ''kokutai'' acquired an additional meaning.
The Government created a whole perfect new cultural system around the Tennou [Emperor], and the ''kokutai'' was the expression of it. Moreover, the ''kokutai'' was the basis of the sovereignty. According to Tatsukichi Minobe, ''kokutai'' is understood as the "shape of the Estate" in the sense of "Tenno as the organ of the Estate", while the authoritarians gave the ''kokutai'' a mystical power. The Tennou was a "god" among "humans", the incarnation of the national morals. This notion of ''kokutai'' was extra-juridical, something more cultural than positive. (2006:n.p.)
{{Conservatism in Japan|variants and movements}} This stemmed from drafter [[Itō Hirobumi]]'s rejection of some European notions as unfit for Japan, as they stemmed from European constitutional practice and Christianity.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', pp. 79–80 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} The references to the ''kokutai'' were the justification of the emperor's authority through his divine descent and the unbroken line of emperors, and the unique relationship between subject and sovereign. The "family-state" element in it was given a great deal of prominence by political philosophy.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', p. 80 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} Many conservatives supported these principles as central to '''''Nihon shugi''''' (''Nihon gunkoku shugi'', {{ill|Japanese militarism|en|Japanese militarism|WD=Q702868|lt=Japanese militarism|1=Japanese militarism}}), "Japanism", as an alternative to rapid Westernization.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/427 427–428]|quote=Japanists further circumscribed the permissible limits of political discourse. From the middleof the Meiji period, some conservatives had begun to advocate Nihon shugi, or Japanism, as an alternative to rapid Westernization. In particular, they wished to preserve traditional values and what they saw as Japan's unique national polity, or kokutai. For many conservatives in the Meiji era, the concept of the kokutai revolved around two principles. A divine line of emperors had ruled from time immemorial, and intimate familylike ties united the benevolent sovereign with his loyal subjects.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/427}} ''Nihon shugi'' (日本主義, lit. "Japan-ism") is an ideology that values the traditional Japanese spirit and sets the tone of the state and society; it emerged in this period as a reaction to the {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}'s radical [[:en:Europeanization|Europeanization]] policy.{{cite web |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E4%B8%BB%E7%BE%A9-110186#E5.A4.A7.E8.BE.9E.E6.9E.97.20.E7.AC.AC.E4.B8.89.E7.89.88 |title=日本主義 |access-date=12 March 2024 |website=kotobank.jp |language=ja }} Nihon shugi is a kind of "''kukka shugi''" (国家主義, lit. "statism" or "nationalism") ideology. ''Nihon Shugi'' opposed 'Europeanism' (欧化主義), '{{ill|Democracy|en|Democracy|WD=Q7174|lt=Democracy|1=Democracy}}' and '{{ill|Socialism|en|Socialism|WD=Q7272|lt=Socialism|1=Socialism}}', which were considered unrelated to Japanese traditions, and during the {{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taishō|1=Taishō era}} and {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era|1=Shōwa era}}, it emphasized the ''Kokutai'' ideology centered on the emperor as opposed to {{ill|Marxism|en|Marxism|WD=Q7264|lt=Marxism|1=Marxism}}. ===Taishō Democracy=== From the [[:en:Xinhai Revolution|Xinhai Revolution]] to the enactment of the {{ill|Peace Preservation Law|en|Peace Preservation Law|WD=Q657216|lt=Peace Preservation Law|1=Peace Preservation Law}} (1911–1925), the most important pre-World War II democracy movement "[[:en:Taisho Democracy|Taishō Democracy]]" occurred. During the Taishō Democracy, the political theorist {{ill|Sakuzō Yoshino|en|Sakuzō Yoshino|WD=Q1186931|lt=Sakuzō Yoshino|1=Sakuzō Yoshino}} (1878–1933) rejected Western democracy ''minshu shugi'' (民主主義 lit. "people rule principle/-ism") and proposed a compromise on imperial democracy ''minpon shugi'' (民本主義 "people based principle/-ism"). However, as {{ill|Japanese nationalism|en|Japanese nationalism|WD=Q1331440|lt=Japanese nationalism|1=Japanese nationalism}} grew, questions arose whether the ''kokutai'' emperor could be limited by the ''seitai'' government. The {{ill|Peace Preservation Law|en|Peace Preservation Law|WD=Q657216|lt=Peace Preservation Law|1=Peace Preservation Law}} of 1925 forbade both forming and belonging to any organization that proposed altering the ''kokutai'' or the abolishment of private property, effectively criminalizing socialism, communism, {{ill|Republicanism|en|Republicanism|WD=Q877848|lt=Republicanism|1=Republicanism}}, democracy and other anti-Tenno [[:en:ideologies|ideologies]].{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/390 390]|quote=At the same time that [the government] approved universal manhood suffrage, the Diet passed the Peace Preservation Law of 1925. Drafted by bureaucrats within the Ministry of Justice, the measure stipulated that anyone "who organizes a group for the purpose of changing the national polity (kokutai) or of denying the private property system, or anyone who knowingly participates in such group" could be jailed for ten years, or even executed after the law was amended three years later.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/390}} The [[:en:Tokubetsu Kōtō Keisatsu|Tokkō]] ("Special Higher Police") was established as a type of {{ill|Thought Police|en|Thought Police|WD=Q1264653|lt=Thought Police|1=Thought Police}} to investigate political groups that might threaten Tenno-centered social order of Japan.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', p. 184 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} ===World War II usage=== {{ill|Tatsukichi Minobe|en|Tatsukichi Minobe|WD=Q709643|lt=Tatsukichi Minobe|1=Tatsukichi Minobe}} (1873–1948), a professor emeritus of law at {{ill|University of Tokyo|en|University of Tokyo|WD=Q7842|lt=Tokyo Imperial University|1=University of Tokyo}}, theorized that under the Meiji Constitution, the emperor was an organ of the state and not a sacrosanct power beyond the state.{{ill|Andrew Gordon (historian)|en|Andrew Gordon (historian)|WD=Q4757131|lt=Andrew Gordon|1=Andrew Gordon (historian)}}, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', pp. 198–199, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} This was regarded as ''{{ill|Lèse-majesté|en|Lèse-majesté|WD=Q1134057|lt=Lèse-majesté|1=Lèse-majesté}}''.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/428 428]|quote=In the 1930s, however, Japanists singled out Minobe for intense criticism. Battle was joined in 1934 when rightwing organizations, including the Imperial Military Reservists' Association, published accusatory books and pamphlets charging that Minobe's thoughts amounted to Ièse majesté.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/428}} Minobe was appointed to the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}} in 1932 but forced to resign after an assassination attempt and vehement criticisms that he was disloyal to the emperor.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', p. 199, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} Great efforts were made to foment a "Japanese spirit" even in popular culture, as in the promotion of the "{{ill|Ode of Showa Restoration|en|Ode of Showa Restoration|WD=Q30947150|lt=Song of Young Japan|1=Ode of Showa Restoration}}."{{ill|Piers Brendon|en|Piers Brendon|WD=Q15458673|lt=Piers Brendon|1=Piers Brendon}}, ''The Dark Valley: A Panorama of the 1930s'', p. 441 {{ISBN|0-375-40881-9}}
Brave warriors united in justice In spirit a match for a million – Ready like the myriad {{ill|Cherry blossom|en|Cherry blossom|WD=Q871991|lt=Cherry blossom|1=Cherry blossom}}s to scatter In the spring sky of the {{ill|Shōwa Restoration|en|Shōwa Restoration|WD=Q863412|lt=Shōwa Restoration|1=Shōwa Restoration}}.
The national debates over ''kokutai'' led the Prime Minister Prince {{ill|Fumimaro Konoe|en|Fumimaro Konoe|WD=Q315594|lt=Fumimaro Konoe|1=Fumimaro Konoe}} to appoint a committee of Japan's leading professors to deliberate the matter. In 1937, they issued the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' (国体の本義, "Cardinal Principles of the National Body/Structure", see Gauntlett and Hall 1949). Miller gives this description.
The document known as the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' was actually a pamphlet of 156 pages, an official publication of the {{ill|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|en|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|WD=Q1054379|lt=Japanese Ministry of Education|1=Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology}}, first issued in March 1937 and eventually circulated in millions of copies throughout the home islands and the empire. It contained the official teaching of the Japanese state on every aspect of domestic policy, international affairs, culture, and civilization. (1982:92)
It clearly stated its purpose: to overcome social unrest and to develop a new Japan.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/465 465–466]|quote=Besides hushing its critics, the government sought to inculcate good citizenship among schoolchildren by introducing a new textbook, Kokutai no hongi ("Cardinal Principles of the National Polity"), published by the Ministry of Education on March 30, 1937, as an official statement of the government's concept of the kokutai. The purpose of the text, according to its own conclusion, was to overcome social unrest and "develop a new Japan by virtue of the Way of the Empire which stands firm throughout the ages at home and abroad, and thereby more than ever to guard and maintain the prosperity of the Imperial Throne which is coeval with heaven and earth." Following a historical overview that paid special honor to the divine origins of the imperial line, a series of overtly nationalistic essays explored the vlrtues of Japan's "special and unique" customs, culture, religion, morality, and way of life. Throughout the volume, the prose sang the praises of the national achievements of the past, credited those accomplishments to the wisdom of the imperial house, and called upon the Japanese of the 1930s to prepare themselves to make any sacrifice necessary to preserve the integrity of the emperor and nation.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/465}} From this pamphlet, pupils were taught to put the nation before the self, and that they were part of the state and not separate from it.W. G. Beasley, ''The Rise of Modern Japan'', p. 187 {{ISBN|0-312-04077-6}} It also instructed them in the principle of [[hakkō ichiu]] ("eight cords, one roof"), which would be used to justify imperialism.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/470 470]|quote=Konoe and Matsuoka added to the allure of a geographically extended coprosperity sphere by wrapping it in imperial shrouds. Any move south, they averred, would be accomplished "peacefully" and in accordance, as Konoe so carefully phrased it in his radio address, "with the lofty spirit of hakko ichiu." It was another skillful rhetorical flourish by the veteran wordsmith. As every Japanese schoolchild who had read Kokutai no hongi knew by heart, hakko ichiu meant "eight cords, one roof" and first appeared in the eighth-century chronicle [[Nihon Shoki]] to describe how the legendary first emperor Jimmu extended his dominion over the other clans of the early Japanese islands, which subsequently enjoyed unparalleled prosperity and security thanks to his imperial benevolence. Superimposed upon Asia in 1940, the resuscitated ideal pictured a quasi family of nations led by Japan and its patriarch-emperor; the "Imperial Way," Matsuoka intoned, would permit "every nation and every race" to find "its proper place in the world."|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/470}} Brownlee concludes that after the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' proclamation,
It is clear that at this stage in history, they were no longer dealing with a concept to generate spiritual unity like Aizawa Seishisai in 1825, or with a political theory of Japan designed to accommodate modern institutions of government, like the Meiji Constitution. The committee of professors from prestigious universities sought to define the essential truths of Japan, which might be termed religious, or even metaphysical, because they required faith at the expense of logic and reason. (2006:13)
The Ministry of Education promulgated it throughout the school system. By 1937, "election purification", originally aimed at corruption, required that no candidate set the people in opposition to either the military or the bureaucracy.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', p. 196, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} This was required because voters were required to support imperial rule. Some objections to the founding of the ''Taisei Yokusankai'' or {{ill|Imperial Rule Assistance Association|en|Imperial Rule Assistance Association|WD=Q714797|lt=Imperial Rule Assistance Association|1=Imperial Rule Assistance Association}}, came on the grounds that ''kokutai'' already required all imperial subjects to support imperial rule. Conservative thinkers voiced concerns that the establishment of an empowered class of aides to the emperor was akin to the creation of a new shogunate.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/454 454]|quote=Conservatives such as Hiranuma Kiichiro, who served as prime minister for eight months in 1939, objected that the proposed totalitarian IRAA was nothing but a "new shogunate" that would usurp the power of the emperor's government, and Japanists declared that the national polity, the hallowed kokutai, already united the emperor with subjects who naturally fulfilled their sacred obligation to "assist imperial rule." On a more mundane plane, senior officials within the Home Ministry feared the loss of bureaucratic turf and complained that the proposed network of occupationally based units would interfere with local administration at a particularly crucial time in the nation's history.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/454}} For the leaders of Japan's "fascist-nationalist clique", writes Miller (1982:93), "''kokutai'' had become a convenient term for indicating all the ways in which they believed that the Japanese nation, as a political as well as a racial entity, was simultaneously different from and superior to all other nations on earth." This term, and what it meant, were widely inculcated in propaganda.Anthony Rhodes, ''Propaganda: The art of persuasion: World War II'', p. 246, 1976, Chelsea House Publishers, New York The final letters of {{ill|Kamikaze|en|Kamikaze|WD=Q133194|lt=Kamikaze|1=Kamikaze}} pilots expressed, above all, that their motivations were gratitude to Japan and to its Emperor as the embodiment of ''kokutai''.{{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris|1=Ivan Morris}}, ''The Nobility of Failure: Tragic Heroes in the History of Japan'', p. 309 Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1975 {{ISBN?}} A sailor might give his life to save the picture of the Emperor on a submarine.{{ill|Masanori Ito (journalist)|en|Masanori Ito (journalist)|WD=Q10885109|lt=Masanori Ito|1=Masanori Itō (journalist)}}, ''The End of the Imperial Japanese Navy'' p. 28, New York W.W. Norton & Company, 1956 During World War II, some anti-{{ill|Modernism|en|Modernism|WD=Q878985|lt=modernist|1=Modernism}} intellectuals argued that prior to the [[Meiji Restoration]], Japan was always a classless society under a benevolent emperor, but the restoration had plunged the nation into Western materialism (an argument that ignored commercialism and ribald culture in the Tokugawa era), which had caused people to forget their nature. To recover their traditional identity, Japanese citizens had to actively participate in the war effort.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', pp. 219–220, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} "Japanist" unions endeavoured to win support by disavowing class violence and pledging support for nation and emperor.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/467 467]|quote=The growing sense of national emergency prompted many groups that earlier had assumed an oppositional stance toward the state to reassess their goals and tactics. One expression of that tendency came in the early 1930s, when thousands of workers joined so-called Japanist unions whose leadership hoped to improve working conditions by disavowing violent confrontations and demonstrating their loyalty to nation and emperor. Kamino Shin'ichi, originally a foreman at the lshikawajima shipyards, organized one of the more influential Japanist unions. In concert with other members of the conservative right, he and his followers ridiculed the political parties as being corrupt, condemned liberalism and democracy as the failed ideologies of a decadent West, and sought to build a new industrial order, premised on the "unity of emperor and subject," in which laborers and capitalists would be "of one mind and spirit, fused in an inseparable solidarity."|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/467}} Nevertheless, because of the mistrust of unions in such unity, the Japanese went to replace them with "councils" in every factory, containing both management and worker representatives to contain conflict.Andrew Gordon, ''A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa to the Present'', pp. 195–196, {{ISBN|0-19-511060-9}}, {{OCLC|49704795}} Like the Nazi councils they were copying, this was part of a program to create a classless national unity. Because many religions had figures that distracted from the central emperor, they were attacked, such as the [[Oomoto]] sect condemned for worshipping figures other than [[Amaterasu]], and in 1939, the Religious Organization authorized the shutting down of any religion that did not conform to the Imperial Way, which the authorities promptly used.{{Cite book|title=Japan: A Modern History|last=McClain|first=James L.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.|year=2002|isbn=0393041565|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/469 469]|quote=No group experienced more severe suppression than the new religions as Home Ministry bureaucrats embarked upon a crusade "to eradicate evil cults" for the crime of propagating Iese majeste. As manifested in such works as kokutai no hongi, the government in the 1930s fostered the growth of an official orthodoxy centered upon a sacrosanct emperor who stood both as the head of state and as the benevolent father of the family of Japanese citizens. Although not overtly antiemperor, many of the new religions espoused doctrines that threatened the centrality of the imperial figure; prosecutors, for instance, condemned the Omoto sect for revering deities other than the Sun Goddess. The most dramatic moment in the government's campaign against "quack religions" came on December 8, 1935, when hundreds of police stormed Omoto headquarters, smashed the main shrine building, dynamited an auxiliary hall, decapitated religious statues, and arrested nearly a thousand sect members. Four years later the Diet passed the Religious Organizations Law empowering the government to disband any religious organization whose teachings did not conform with "The Imperial Way," and officials promptly suppressed other unorthodox religions. An aversion for social disorder and a desire to "unify the will of the people" around national goals prompted bureaucratic officials in the 1930s to suppress or to co-opt the support of organizations that opposed government policies. Some of the associations, notably the Omoto sect, preferred to break rather than to bend, but most tempered their demands, shifted to less contentious goals, or even dissolved themselves.|url=https://archive.org/details/japanmodernhisto00mccl/page/469}} Hirohito evoked the ''Kokutai'' in his {{ill|Hirohito surrender broadcast|en|Hirohito surrender broadcast|WD=Q709465|lt=surrender broadcast|1=Hirohito surrender broadcast}}, which announced the Japanese acceptance of the {{ill|Potsdam Declaration|en|Potsdam Declaration|WD=Q163244|lt=Potsdam Declaration|1=Potsdam Declaration}} (unconditional surrender). ==Post-1945== By the {{ill|Surrender of Japan|en|Surrender of Japan|WD=Q6540361|lt=Surrender of Japan|1=Surrender of Japan}} in 1945, the significance of ''kokutai'' diminished. In autumn 1945, [[:en:Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers|GHQ]] forbade circulation of the ''Kokutai no Hongi'' and on 15 October repealed the 1925 {{ill|Peace Preservation Law|en|Peace Preservation Law|WD=Q657216|lt=Peace Preservation Law|1=Peace Preservation Law}}. By the enactment of the {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|WD=Q237082|lt=Constitution of the State of Japan|1=Constitution of Japan}} (3 May 1947), {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Tenno|1=Emperor of Japan}}'s sovereignty and the ''lèse-majesté'' were repealed. Nevertheless, some authors, including Miller (1982:95), believe that traces of Japanese ''kokutai'' "are quite as vivid today as they ever were". In the 21st century, Japanese nationalists, such as those affiliated with the {{ill|Nippon Kaigi|en|Nippon Kaigi|WD=Q11507216|lt=Nippon Kaigi|1=Nippon Kaigi}} lobby, have begun using the phrase "kunigara" (国柄, "national character"). == Notes == :1.{{note|a}}In the illustration is the "Tokoyo no Naganakidori" (常世之長鳴鳥), a long-singing [[:en:cockerel|cockerel]] from the {{illm|Everlasting Land|ja|常世の国}} which appears in the [[Kojiki]] as the herald of Amaterasu. == See also == {{Portal|Japan}} *''{{ill|An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus|en|An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus|WD=Q4750110|lt=An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus|1=An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus}}'' *{{ill|Gekokujō|en|Gekokujō|WD=Q2416571|lt=Gekokujō|1=Gekokujō}} *[[Imperial Rescript on Education]] *{{ill|Japanese Historical Text Initiative|en|Japanese Historical Text Initiative|WD=Q16973361|lt=Japanese Historical Text Initiative|1=Japanese Historical Text Initiative}} *{{ill|Hirohito surrender broadcast|en|Hirohito surrender broadcast|WD=Q709465|lt=Hirohito surrender broadcast|1=Hirohito surrender broadcast}} (Gyokuon-hōsō) *{{ill|Kokuchūkai|en|Kokuchūkai|WD=Q11420994|lt=Kokuchūkai|1=Kokuchūkai}} (Column of the Nation Society) *[[National Spiritual Mobilization Movement]] *[[Shinbutsu-shūgō]] *[[:en:Socialist thought in Imperial Japan|Socialist thought in Imperial Japan]] *[[:en:Statism in Shōwa Japan|Statism in Shōwa Japan]] *{{ill|Uyoku dantai|en|Uyoku dantai|WD=Q181924|lt=Uyoku dantai|1=Uyoku dantai}} (Nationalist groups of Japan) *{{ill|Yangmingism|en|Yangmingism|WD=Q697205|lt=Yangmingism|1=Yangmingism}} *{{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine|1=Yasukuni Shrine}} == References == {{reflist}} * Brownlee, John S. "[http://www.adilegian.com/PDF/brownlee.pdf Four Stages of the Japanese Kokutai (National Essence)]", 2000. * Daikichi, Irokawa. ''The Culture of the Meiji Period''. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1970. * Gauntlett, John Owen and Hall, Robert King. ''Kokutai no hongi: cardinal principles of the national entity of Japan''. Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University press, 1949. * {{ill|Joseph Kitagawa|en|Joseph Kitagawa|WD=Q3185165|lt=Kitagawa, Joseph M.|1=Joseph Kitagawa}} "The Japanese ''Kokutai'' (National Community) History and Myth", ''History of Religions'', Vol. 13.3 (Feb., 1974), pp. 209–226. * Valderrama López, Josefa. "[http://seneca.uab.cat/hmic/2006/orientats/Kokutai.pdf Beyond words: the "kokutai" and its background]{{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}". ''Història Moderna i Contemporània'', 2006. {{ISSN|1696-4403}}. * Miller, Roy Andrew. ''Japan's Modern Myth''. New York: Weatherhill, 1982. * Antoni, Klaus ''Kokutai – Political Shintô from Early-Modern to Contemporary Japan''. Eberhard Karls University Tuebingen, Tobias-lib 2016. {{ISBN|978-3-946552-00-0}}.
